title_en: Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases on Trademark Granting and Confirmation of Rights

articles.content_en: Article 1: For the purposes of these Provisions, administrative cases concerning trademark authorization and confirmation refer to cases in which a counterpart or an interested party, dissatisfied with administrative acts made by the National Intellectual Property Administration, such as trademark refusal review, trademark non-registration review, trademark revocation review, trademark invalidation declaration, and invalidation declaration review, initiates prosecution with the People's Court.

Article 2: The scope of review by the People's Court of administrative acts concerning trademark authorization and confirmation shall generally be determined based on the plaintiff's litigation claims and reasons. Where the plaintiff has not raised any claim in the lawsuit, but the relevant determination of the National Intellectual Property Administration is clearly improper, the People's Court may, after the parties have presented their opinions, review the relevant matters and render a judgment.

Article 3: The 'identical or similar' to the name of the People's Republic of China and other matters as prescribed in Item (1) of the First Paragraph of Article 10 of the Trademark Law means that the trademark mark is identical or similar to the state name and other matters as a whole.
For a mark containing the name of the People's Republic of China and other matters but which is not identical or similar as a whole, if the registration of such mark as a trademark may damage the dignity of the state, the People's Court may determine that it falls under the circumstances prescribed in Item (8) of the First Paragraph of Article 10 of the Trademark Law.

Article 4: Where a trademark mark or its constituent elements is deceptive and is likely to cause the public to misidentify the characteristics such as quality or the place of origin of the goods, and the National Intellectual Property Administration determines that it falls under the circumstances prescribed in Item (7) of the First Paragraph of Article 10 of the Trademark Law as amended in 2001, the People's Court shall support it.

Article 5: Where a trademark mark or its constituent elements may have a negative or adverse impact on the social public interests and public order of China, the People's Court may determine that it falls under the 'other adverse influences' prescribed in Item (8) of the First Paragraph of Article 10 of the Trademark Law.
Applying for registration of the names of public figures in the fields of politics, economy, culture, religion, ethnicity, etc. as trademarks falls under the 'other adverse influences' referred to in the preceding paragraph.

Article 6: Where a trademark mark consists of a place name of an administrative division at or above the county level or a foreign place name known to the public and other elements, if it has a meaning distinct from the place name as a whole, the People's Court shall determine that it does not fall under the circumstances referred to in the Second Paragraph of Article 10 of the Trademark Law.

Article 7: When examining whether the trademark in dispute has distinctiveness, the People's Court shall, according to the general understanding of the relevant public of the goods for which the trademark is designated for use, determine whether the trademark as a whole has distinctiveness. Where a trademark mark contains descriptive elements but this does not affect its distinctiveness as a whole; or where a descriptive mark is presented in a unique manner and the relevant public can identify the source of the goods through it, it shall be determined that the trademark has distinctiveness.

Article 8: Where the trademark in dispute is a foreign-language mark, the People's Court shall, according to the general understanding of the relevant public within China, examine and determine whether the foreign-language trademark has distinctiveness. The inherent meaning of the foreign language in the mark may affect its distinctiveness on the designated goods, but if the relevant public has a relatively low degree of cognition of such inherent meaning and can use the mark to identify the source of the goods, it may be determined that the mark has distinctiveness.

Article 9: Where an application for trademark registration is filed for a three-dimensional mark consisting solely of the shape of the goods itself or a part of the shape of the goods itself, and the relevant public generally does not easily recognize it as a sign indicating the source of the goods, such three-dimensional mark does not have distinctiveness as a trademark.
The fact that the shape is original or first used by the applicant shall not automatically lead to its distinctiveness as a trademark.
Where the mark referred to in the First Paragraph has been used for a long or extensive period and the relevant public can identify the source of the goods through the mark, it may be determined that the mark has distinctiveness.

Article 10: Where the trademark in dispute is a statutory commodity name or a customary commodity name, the People's Court shall determine that it is the generic name referred to in Item (1) of the First Paragraph of Article 11 of the Trademark Law. Where it belongs to a generic commodity name in accordance with legal provisions or national standards or industry standards, it shall be determined as a generic name. Where the relevant public generally considers that a certain name can refer to a category of goods, it shall be determined as a customary generic name. Where it is listed as a commodity name in professional reference books, dictionaries, etc., it may be used as a reference for determining a customary generic name.
A customary generic name shall generally be judged according to the general understanding of the relevant public nationwide. For goods with a fixed relevant market formed due to historical traditions, local customs, geographical environment, and other reasons, the People's Court may determine the appellation commonly used within the relevant market as a generic name.
Where the applicant for the trademark in dispute knows or should have known that the trademark applied for registration is a customary commodity name in part of the region, the People's Court may regard the trademark applied for registration as a generic name.
When the People's Court reviews and determines whether the trademark in dispute is a generic name, it shall generally take the factual state at the date of trademark application as the standard. If the factual state changes at the time of approval of registration, whether it is a generic name shall be judged based on the factual state at the time of approval of registration.

Article 11: Where a trademark mark merely or mainly describes or explains the quality, main raw materials, functions, purposes, weight, quantity, place of origin, etc. of the goods on which it is used, the People's Court shall determine that it falls under the circumstances prescribed in Item (2) of the First Paragraph of Article 11 of the Trademark Law. Where a trademark mark or its constituent elements suggests the characteristics of the goods but does not affect its function of identifying the source of the goods, it shall not fall under the circumstances prescribed in that item.

Article 14: Where a party claims that the trademark in dispute constitutes a reproduction, imitation, or translation of its registered well-known trademark and therefore shall not be registered or shall be invalidated, and the National Intellectual Property Administration has ruled in support of such claim in accordance with Article 30 of the Trademark Law, if the registration of the trademark in dispute has not exceeded five years, the People's Court may, after the parties have stated their opinions, conduct the trial in accordance with Article 30 of the Trademark Law; if the registration of the trademark in dispute has exceeded five years, the Third Paragraph of Article 13 of the Trademark Law shall apply.

Article 15: Where a trademark agent or representative, or an agent or representative in the sense of a distribution, agency or other sales agency relationship, without authorization, applies for registration in its own name of a trademark identical or similar to the trademark of the principal or the represented person on identical or similar goods, the People's Court shall apply the provisions of the First Paragraph of Article 15 of the Trademark Law for trial.
Where, at the stage of negotiations for establishing an agency or representative relationship, the agent or representative referred to in the preceding paragraph applies for registration of the trademark of the principal or the represented person, the People's Court shall apply the provisions of the First Paragraph of Article 15 of the Trademark Law for trial.
Where there is a specific identity relationship such as kinship between the trademark applicant and the agent or representative, it may be presumed that the trademark registration act is malicious collusion with the agent or representative, and the People's Court shall apply the provisions of the First Paragraph of Article 15 of the Trademark Law for trial.

Article 17: Where an interested party in a geographical indication, in accordance with Article 16 of the Trademark Law, claims that another person's trademark shall not be registered or shall be invalidated, if the goods designated for use by the trademark in dispute are not the same goods as the geographical indication product, but the interested party in the geographical indication can prove that the use of the trademark in dispute on the product still easily causes the relevant public to mistakenly believe that the product originates from the region and therefore has specific quality, reputation, or other characteristics, the People's Court shall support it.
If the geographical indication has been registered as a collective mark or certification mark, the right holder or interested party of the collective mark or certification mark may choose to claim rights in accordance with that article, or separately in accordance with Article 13, Article 30, etc. of the Trademark Law.

Article 18: The prior rights prescribed in Article 32 of the Trademark Law include the civil rights or other legitimate rights and interests that a party enjoyed prior to the application date of the trademark in dispute. Where the prior rights no longer exist at the time the trademark in dispute is approved for registration, this shall not affect the registration of the trademark in dispute.

Article 19: Where a party claims that the trademark in dispute infringes its prior copyright, the People's Court shall, in accordance with the Copyright Law and other relevant provisions, review whether the claimed subject matter constitutes a work, whether the party is the copyright owner or other interested party entitled to claim copyright, and whether the trademark in dispute constitutes an infringement of copyright.
Where the trademark mark constitutes a work protected by the Copyright Law, the design drafts, originals, contracts for obtaining rights, and copyright registration certificates prior to the application date of the trademark in dispute provided by the party may all serve as prima facie evidence of copyright ownership.
Trademark announcements, trademark registration certificates, etc. may serve as prima facie evidence for determining that the trademark applicant is an interested party entitled to claim copyright in the trademark mark.

Article 20: Where a party claims that the trademark in dispute infringes its right to name, if the relevant public believes that the trademark mark refers to that natural person and is likely to believe that the goods bearing the trademark are licensed by that natural person or have a specific connection with that natural person, the People's Court shall determine that the trademark infringes the right to name of that natural person.
Where a party claims the right to name based on a specific name such as a pen name, stage name, or translated name, if such specific name has a certain degree of fame and has established a stable corresponding relationship with the natural person, and the relevant public uses it to refer to the natural person, the People's Court shall support it.

Article 21: Where the trade name claimed by a party has a certain degree of market fame, and another person applies for registration, without authorization, of a trademark identical or similar to that trade name, which is likely to cause confusion among the relevant public as to the source of the goods, and the party claims that this constitutes a prior right and interest, the People's Court shall support it.
Where a party makes a claim based on an abbreviation of an enterprise name that has a certain degree of market fame and has established a stable corresponding relationship with the enterprise, the provisions of the preceding paragraph shall apply.

Article 22: Where a party claims that the trademark in dispute infringes the copyright in a character image, the People's Court shall conduct the review in accordance with Article 19 of these Provisions.
For a work within the term of copyright protection, if the title of the work, the name of the character in the work, etc. have relatively high fame, and the use of the name as a trademark on relevant goods is likely to cause the relevant public to mistakenly believe that it has been licensed by the right holder or has a specific connection with the right holder, if the party claims that this constitutes a prior right and interest, the People's Court shall support it.

Article 23: Where a prior user claims that the trademark applicant, by improper means, preemptively registered a trademark that the prior user has used and has a certain influence, if the prior-used trademark has a certain influence, and the trademark applicant knew or should have known of the trademark, it may be presumed that the applicant has constituted 'preemptive registration by improper means'. However, this shall not apply where the trademark applicant proves that it had no malice in exploiting the goodwill of the prior-used trademark.
Where the prior user proves that its prior trademark has a certain continuous period of use, region, sales volume, or advertising, the People's Court may determine that it has a certain influence.
Where the prior user claims that the trademark applicant applied for registration of a trademark that the prior user has used and has a certain influence on goods not similar to its goods, violating Article 32 of the Trademark Law, the People's Court shall not support it.

Article 24: Where a person disrupts the order of trademark registration, harms public interests, improperly occupies public resources, or seeks improper interests by means other than deceptive means, the People's Court may determine that this falls under the 'other improper means' prescribed in the First Paragraph of Article 44 of the Trademark Law.

Article 25: When the People's Court determines whether the applicant for the trademark in dispute has 'maliciously registered' another person's well-known trademark, it shall comprehensively consider the fame of the cited trademark, the reasons for the applicant's application for the trademark in dispute, and the specific circumstances of the use of the trademark in dispute to determine the applicant's subjective intent. Where the cited trademark has high fame and the applicant for the trademark in dispute has no justifiable reason, the People's Court may presume that its registration constitutes 'malicious registration' referred to in the First Paragraph of Article 45 of the Trademark Law.

Article 26: Use by the trademark right holder itself, use by others with permission, and other use that does not contravene the will of the trademark right holder may all be recognized as use as referred to in the Second Paragraph of Article 49 of the Trademark Law.
Where the trademark mark actually used differs subtly from the trademark mark approved for registration, but the distinctive characteristics have not been changed, it may be regarded as use of the registered trademark.
Where there is no actual use of the registered trademark and only assignment or licensing acts exist; or where there is only publication of trademark registration information and declaration of the exclusive right to use the registered trademark, this shall not be recognized as trademark use.
Where the trademark right holder has a genuine intention to use the trademark and has made necessary preparations for actual use, but has not yet actually used the registered trademark due to other objective reasons, the People's Court may determine that it has justifiable reasons.

Article 28: In the process of the People's Court's trial of an administrative case concerning trademark authorization and confirmation, if the grounds for the National Intellectual Property Administration's refusal, refusal to approve registration, or declaration of invalidation of the trademark in dispute no longer exist, the People's Court may, based on new facts, revoke the relevant ruling of the National Intellectual Property Administration and order it to make a new ruling based on the changed facts.

Article 29: A review application filed by a party based on evidence newly discovered after the original administrative act, or evidence that could not be obtained due to objective reasons or could not be provided within the prescribed time limit during the original administrative procedure, or new legal grounds, shall not be deemed to be a repeated review application 'with the same facts and reasons'.
In a trademark refusal review procedure, after the National Intellectual Property Administration approves the preliminary examination announcement of the application trademark on the grounds that the application trademark and the cited trademark do not constitute identical or similar trademarks used on the same or similar goods, the following circumstances shall not be regarded as a repeated review application 'with the same facts and reasons':
(1) the owner of the cited trademark or an interested party files an opposition based on the cited trademark, the National Intellectual Property Administration supports it, and the applicant of the opposed trademark applies for review;
(2) the owner of the cited trademark or an interested party, after the application trademark is approved for registration, applies for a declaration of invalidation of the application trademark based on the cited trademark.

Article 30: Where a final and effective judgment of the People's Court has made clear determinations on the relevant facts and application of law, and a counterpart or interested party initiates prosecution against a ruling newly made by the National Intellectual Property Administration in accordance with that effective judgment, the People's Court shall, according to law, rule that the case shall not be accepted; if it has already been accepted, it shall rule to dismiss the prosecution.

Article 31: These Provisions shall come into force on March 1, 2017. Administrative cases concerning trademark authorization and confirmation tried by the People's Court in accordance with the Trademark Law as amended in 2001 may apply these Provisions by reference.
